explanation: Fires on the first subword piece of a verb that the tokenizer splits into several pieces (e.g. 'sp|üren', ' begin|nt', ' erk|ennen', 're|oc|cur', ' exacerb|ate', ' res|usc|itate'). It works across languages (German, Dutch, English). Whole-word verbs and function words give little or no activation.

A mixture with no clear common thread. It fires on the head noun or word that completes a set phrase ('deadly force', 'bring to the table', 'mental health problems', 'made the mistake', 'on line 130'), on stat/math subscripts like 'p', and on pieces of code identifiers (HOMEDRIVE, romanToInt, "('").

Fires on the word that introduces who a statement, judgment or action comes from: agentive 'by' after a passive verb ('condemned by', 'announced by', 'described by'), and headline attribution verbs like ', says X' or ', warns X', plus similar uses of 'for', 'from' and 'told'. Other uses of 'by' or prepositions give weak or no activation.

No clear pattern. Strong examples include legal opinion boilerplate ('O R D E R', 'appellee', 'remanded', 'estoppel', 'JUDGMENT'), code and LLVM tokens, gene or abbreviation fragments, and foreign-word fragments.

Mainly fires on the noun that names a person's role in a sports biography, especially 'footballer', 'soccer player' or 'football player' after nationality and birth details. It also fires on nearby sports-roster context and on 'person'-type words ('Personnel', 'Sportspeople', 'Personal history'). It is weaker on general mentions of people.

Fires mostly on prepositions or function words that link the parts of a multi-word name or phrase ('University of', 'University in St. Louis', 'Schools of Excellence', 'Segunda División de', 'removed from', 'stock in'). It also fires on assorted separators in code, paths and numbers ('/', ' -', '+\'). The common factor is weak, so it is hard to predict.

A mixture: 'post' in time expressions ('120 h post inoculation', 'year post-menopause'), question marks ending a question before a new line, pronoun objects ('hold it', 'hold them'), 'look', and URL or identifier fragments. No single rule predicts it.

Fires on a function word or small word inside a common multi-word expression, at the point where the idiom is being completed ('take it for', 'take this for granted', 'a little easier', 'on-base', 'epithelial-to-mesenchymal', 'went the predicted way'). The examples are heterogeneous, so it is hard to predict.

Fires on subword fragments inside rare or foreign words and proper names (Polish, Slovene and Czech words, Persian place names, Latin taxa, drug names like Lam-iv-udine) and on code or LaTeX identifier fragments. The fragment is often the second piece of the word. Ordinary English words do not activate it.
No coherent pattern. It fires on a score slash ('8/10'), long whitespace runs in legal headers, function words in ordinary prose ('will', 'is', 'other', 'for', 'that'), and code tokens.

Fires on words naming psychoactive substances in the context of use or abuse: 'drug', 'substance', 'Alcohol', 'opiate', 'marijuana', 'smoking'. It is strongest in phrases like 'drug abuse', 'substance abuse' and 'drug use'. It is weaker on related health-behaviour words ('medication', 'adherence', 'contraceptive').

Fires on any form of the verb 'take' (take, takes, taking, taken, took), especially in idiomatic or phrasal uses ('take over', 'take advantage', 'take place', 'take effect', 'taken steps', 'take the job'). Other verbs of action or motion ('leave', 'make', 'earn') get only moderate activation.

A mixture: 'at' in the Boost license phrase 'or copy at', '="' after android:layout_width, '-' in CSS classes like 'col-md-', and mid-clause verbs or function words in prose ('you are using', 'will give', 'able to', 'receive a').

Fires mostly on words about light, imaging and photography: 'light', 'sun', 'camera', 'video', 'refraction', image 'convert', 'weather', 'Film Editing'. There are some unrelated strong hits ('hired ... to design', 'chef', 'Limo').

Fires on the word that opens an embedded clause or list. In prose this is a complementizer or question word after a verb of saying, asking or deciding ('suggesting that', 'decide whether', 'check if', 'Will', 'Are'). In Go code it is the 'import (' opener.

Very sparse. Its one strong hit is 'ip' inside 'immunoprecipitations'. Weaker hits are subword pieces of technical or biochemical terms ('precipitation', 'cross-linked', 'prelim', 'Protocol', drug-name fragments).

Fires on words in expressions of mental capacity, effort or expectation, often inside negated or modal frames: 'keeping track', 'could have dared', 'everything I could', 'never thought', 'no idea', 'hard to imagine', 'can't', 'make every attempt', 'the will'.

Fires on CJK (Chinese or Japanese) characters, especially inside code files, string resources or comments. It also fires moderately on open-source license boilerplate tokens ('AUTHORS OR COPYRIGHT', '**', 'opensource.org').

Fires mainly on the nationality adjective or role word in a short biographical description ('was a German botanist', 'Argentine footballer', 'British composer', 'later became'). It also fires on mid-word pieces of Romance-language words ('com|unit|ario', 'univers|it|ário').

Mostly fires on a subject pronoun or determiner that starts a new clause, especially first and second person ('I', 'you', 'we', 'our', 'your'), after a comma, 'but' or 'wherever'. It also fires on some clause-boundary punctuation. The examples are broad and somewhat noisy.

Fires on a soft-hyphen character inside a word ('mis­leading', 'ser­vices'). It is weaker on the inner piece of compound words and unusual names ('Way|f|aring', 'Pipe|f|itters', "Wet'suwet'en"). It barely responds to anything else.
